questions.questionMd: A researcher reports `p < 0.05` on a Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing two IR systems. A colleague argues this alone is insufficient to conclude that one system is better. Why is the colleague correct?

options.text: A Wilcoxon test requires at least 100 queries before p-values become meaningful, regardless of the result
Statistical significance only rules out chance.
The Wilcoxon test only applies to normally distributed data; using it on MAP scores is methodologically invalid
`p < 0.05` confirms the null hypothesis, meaning the systems perform identically on the query set

questions.explanationMd: A statistically significant result indicates that the observed difference is unlikely to be due to chance, but it does not by itself prove practical importance, effect size, or overall superiority.

questions.questionMd: A search application requires that Recall be weighted more heavily than Precision. Which setting of `β` in the `Fβ` formula achieves this?

options.text: `β = 1`, because this balances Precision and Recall and therefore emphasises neither
`β < 1`, because smaller `β` values shift focus away from Precision toward Recall
`β = 0`, because this setting removes Precision from the calculation entirely
`β > 1`, because larger `β` values increase the weight assigned to Recall in the harmonic mean

questions.explanationMd: In the F-beta measure, values of `β > 1` give more weight to Recall, while values of `β < 1` give more weight to Precision.

questions.questionMd: Why does the phrase query `"machine learning"` return fewer results than the Boolean query `machine AND learning`?

options.text: The phrase query restricts matching to document titles, whereas the Boolean AND searches the full text
The phrase query additionally requires the two terms to appear consecutively in the correct order
The phrase query automatically removes stop words, reducing the candidate set before merging
The phrase query applies a Jaccard similarity threshold that the Boolean AND does not use

questions.explanationMd: A phrase query is stricter because the terms must appear adjacent and in order; Boolean AND only requires both terms to occur somewhere in the document.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, which scenario represents a case where stopword removal should NOT be applied?

options.text: A keyword query for a common technical term like `network`
A phrase query such as `"to be or not to be"`
Indexing a large corpus of general news articles
Preprocessing queries submitted to a web-scale search engine

questions.explanationMd: Stopwords may be meaningful inside phrase queries. Removing them from a phrase such as `to be or not to be` changes the intended match.

questions.questionMd: What is the correct set of 3-grams, with boundary markers, for the vocabulary term `query`?

options.text: `$qu, que, uer, ery`
`qu$, que, uer, ery, ry$`
`$qu, que, uer, ery, ry$`
`$qu, que, uer, ry$`

questions.explanationMd: Adding boundary markers gives `$query$`; its 3-grams are `$qu`, `que`, `uer`, `ery`, and `ry$`.

questions.questionMd: After L2 normalization is applied to all document vectors in the Vector Space Model, what geometric property do all normalized document vectors share?

options.text: All normalized document vectors have the same direction as the query vector for the collection's most common query
All normalized document vectors become orthogonal to one another, eliminating redundant documents
All normalized document vectors are projected onto a two-dimensional plane to enable fast ranking
All normalized document vectors lie on the unit sphere, meaning their Euclidean norm equals 1

questions.explanationMd: L2 normalization scales each vector so its Euclidean length is 1, placing normalized vectors on the unit sphere.

questions.questionMd: In a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) computation, a query returns a ranked list in which no relevant document appears anywhere in the results. What Reciprocal Rank value is assigned to this query?

options.text: The query is excluded from the MRR calculation to avoid distorting the mean
`1.0`, because the metric defaults to the maximum when the query cannot be penalised further
`0.5`, as the midpoint value for a partial retrieval failure
`0.0`, because no relevant document was found

questions.explanationMd: Reciprocal Rank is `1/rank` of the first relevant result. If no relevant result is retrieved, the contribution is defined as `0`.

questions.questionMd: In the complete Boolean query engine described in the lecture, which component is responsible for processing the user's query string immediately before the wildcard resolver?

options.text: The query optimizer, which reorders AND operands by ascending document frequency
The Boolean executor, which performs AND, OR, and NOT postings merges
The query parser, which identifies operators, phrases, and wildcard patterns in the raw input
The spelling corrector, which substitutes misspelled tokens with vocabulary candidates

questions.explanationMd: The parser first interprets the raw query and detects constructs such as operators, phrases, and wildcard patterns; wildcard resolution can then expand wildcard terms.

questions.questionMd: Which sequence correctly represents the order of the seven stages in the standard IR pipeline introduced in Week 1?

options.text: Query Processing → Crawl → Preprocess → Index → Rank → Evaluate → Present
Preprocess → Crawl → Index → Rank → Query Processing → Present → Evaluate
Crawl → Index → Preprocess → Query Processing → Evaluate → Rank → Present
Crawl → Preprocess → Index → Query Processing → Rank → Present → Evaluate

questions.explanationMd: A standard IR pipeline collects documents, preprocesses them, builds the index, processes queries, ranks results, presents them, and then evaluates performance.

questions.questionMd: Compared to Porter stemming, WordNet lemmatization typically achieves a smaller percentage reduction in vocabulary size. Based on the lecture data, approximately what vocabulary reduction does lemmatization achieve versus Porter's `~29%`?

options.text: Approximately `29%`
Approximately `13%`
Approximately `40%`
Approximately `5%`

questions.explanationMd: Lemmatization is more conservative than Porter stemming, so it usually merges fewer word forms and produces a smaller vocabulary reduction.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following best explains why simple whitespace tokenization is insufficient for production search systems?

options.text: It always produces more tokens than a regex-based tokenizer would for the same input
It fails to handle contractions, possessives, URLs, and hyphenated expressions correctly
It requires an external dictionary to identify valid word boundaries
It is too slow for large corpora because it scans the entire text character by character

questions.explanationMd: Production tokenizers must handle punctuation, URLs, contractions, possessives, and hyphenation; splitting only on spaces loses many important cases.

questions.questionMd: A student searches for `"flight delays snow"`. Their actual need is to understand why winter weather disrupts air travel. What does this example best illustrate?

options.text: Information needs can be fully captured in two or three words
Queries and information needs are equivalent when the user is precise
Search engines require queries to match document text exactly
A query is always a lossy compression of the underlying information need

questions.explanationMd: Users often express a richer information need as a short query, so the query loses context and intent.

questions.questionMd: Which formula does BM25 use for the IDF component of a term `t` in a collection of `N` documents with document frequency `df(t)`?

options.text: `log(N / df(t))`

questions.explanationMd: BM25 commonly uses the Robertson-Sparck Jones style smoothed IDF with `+0.5` terms and a `+1` inside the logarithm to keep the value non-negative.

questions.questionMd: What simplifying assumption does the Binary Independence Model (BIM) make about query terms when estimating the probability that a document is relevant?

options.text: Terms are assumed to appear the same number of times in every relevant document in the collection
Terms are assumed to be ranked by their IDF value before any probability estimation is performed
Terms are assumed to have equal document frequency across the entire collection
Terms are assumed to be statistically independent of one another given the relevance status of the document

questions.explanationMd: BIM assumes conditional independence of terms given relevance or non-relevance, which simplifies probabilistic scoring.

questions.questionMd: An OpenSearch query uses `"fields": ["title^3", "body^1"]` inside a `multi_match` clause. What does the `^3` notation mean for the `title` field?

options.text: The query requires at least three matching terms in the `title` field before the document is considered a candidate.
The `title` field is indexed three times to increase recall for title matches.
OpenSearch searches the `title` field three times before falling back to the `body` field.
A match in the `title` field contributes three times more to the relevance score than an equivalent match in the `body` field.

questions.explanationMd: The caret value is a boost. `title^3` gives title matches three times the scoring weight relative to a field with boost 1.

questions.questionMd: An OpenSearch index is created with 3 primary shards. After the index goes into production, the team finds that data has grown and they need more shards. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Increase the replica count, which automatically redistributes documents across more shards.
Update the index settings at runtime to increase the number of primary shards.
Create a new index with the desired shard count and reindex all documents into it.
Use the Shard Split API to divide each existing primary shard into smaller shards without reindexing.

questions.explanationMd: The number of primary shards is fixed for an existing index in the lecture model, so the safe approach is to create a new index with the desired shard count and reindex.

questions.questionMd: In SMART notation, which TF variant assigns a weight of 1 to any term that appears at least once in a document, and 0 to terms that do not appear, completely ignoring how many times the term occurs?

options.text: The augmented variant (symbol `a`), which returns a value in the range `[0.5, 1]`
The Boolean variant (symbol `b`), which returns 1 if `tf > 0` and 0 otherwise
The logarithmic variant (symbol `l`), which returns `1 + log(tf)`
The natural variant (symbol `n`), which returns the raw count `tf(t,d)`

questions.explanationMd: The Boolean TF variant only records whether a term is present or absent, not how often it occurs.

questions.questionMd: PubMed, arXiv, and GitHub Code Search are all examples of which category of IR system?

options.text: Vertical search — domain-specific retrieval over a specialised corpus
Multimedia IR — retrieval using images or audio as the query
Enterprise search — internal document retrieval within an organisation
Conversational IR — answer synthesis rather than ranked document retrieval

questions.explanationMd: These systems search within specialised domains or corpora rather than the entire web.

questions.questionMd: Variable-byte (VB) encoding uses a continuation bit within each byte. What does a continuation bit value of 1, the top bit set, indicate in VB encoding?

options.text: This byte encodes a negative gap and should be subtracted
This byte is a continuation byte and more bytes follow for the current number
This byte marks the boundary between two separate encoded numbers
This is the last (terminal) byte of the current encoded number

questions.explanationMd: In the lecture convention for VB encoding, a top bit of 1 marks the final byte of the current encoded integer.

questions.questionMd: The two-pointer AND merge achieves `O(m + n)` time complexity only because of one crucial property of postings lists. What is that property?

options.text: Postings lists are stored in sorted order of document ID
Postings lists are stored in order of decreasing term frequency
Postings lists contain positional information for each document
Postings lists use variable-byte encoded gaps between document IDs

questions.explanationMd: The linear two-pointer merge works because both postings lists are sorted by document ID, allowing each pointer to advance monotonically.

questions.questionMd: How does a biword index handle a three-word phrase query such as `"machine learning model"`?

options.text: It decomposes the phrase into overlapping biwords and executes an AND query over `machine_learning` and `learning_model`
It falls back to a standard Boolean AND query over the three individual terms
It stores the entire three-word phrase as a single compound dictionary entry
It uses the positional index for any phrase longer than two words

questions.explanationMd: A biword index represents adjacent term pairs. A three-word phrase becomes two overlapping biwords that must both match.

questions.questionMd: A term has a document frequency (DF) of 500 and a term frequency (TF) of 12 in one particular document. What does the DF value of 500 indicate?

options.text: The term appears 500 times across all documents combined
The term's postings list contains 500 position entries
The term appears in documents with an average length of 500 tokens
The term appears in 500 different documents in the corpus

questions.explanationMd: Document frequency counts the number of distinct documents containing the term, not the total number of occurrences.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, when is the `avgdl` (average document length) statistic used by BM25 computed?

options.text: Each time a new document is added to the index, `avgdl` is recomputed from scratch
At query time by averaging the lengths of all retrieved candidate documents
Only during evaluation when comparing BM25 against TF-IDF outputs
Once at index construction time and stored as a collection-level statistic

questions.explanationMd: BM25 needs collection-level statistics such as average document length, which are computed during indexing and stored for retrieval-time scoring.

questions.questionMd: Using VB encoding, a gap value of 5 requires how many bytes, and a gap value of 200 requires how many bytes?

options.text: 1 byte for gap 5 and 1 byte for gap 200
1 byte for gap 5 and 2 bytes for gap 200
2 bytes for gap 5 and 2 bytes for gap 200
2 bytes for gap 5 and 4 bytes for gap 200

questions.explanationMd: A gap of 5 fits in one 7-bit payload. A gap of 200 exceeds 127, so it needs two VB bytes.

questions.questionMd: How does BM25's approach to document length normalization differ from the cosine-based L2 normalization used in the Vector Space Model?

options.text: BM25 applies length normalization only to query terms, whereas L2 normalization is applied only to document vectors
BM25 applies per-term length normalization controlled by the parameter `b`
BM25 normalizes by the document's maximum term frequency, while L2 normalization normalizes by the sum of all term frequencies
BM25 removes length normalization entirely, relying solely on TF saturation to control the influence of document length

questions.explanationMd: BM25 normalizes each term contribution using document length, average document length, and the parameter `b`, rather than normalizing the entire vector to unit length.

questions.questionMd: Which BM25 variant is specifically designed to handle structured documents that contain multiple distinct fields such as title, body, and anchor text?

options.text: BM25L, which modifies the IDF component for improved handling of very long documents
BM25F, which assigns a separate length normalization parameter `b` and weight to each field
BM25+, which adds a lower bound to the TF contribution to avoid over-penalizing long relevant documents
BM25 with `b = 0`, which disables length normalization across all document fields

questions.explanationMd: BM25F extends BM25 to fielded documents by allowing different field weights and field-specific normalization.

questions.questionMd: Heap's Law states that vocabulary grows sub-linearly with corpus size. Which of the following engineering decisions is most directly motivated by this property?

options.text: Indexing systems must support incremental updates
The entire index can be built in a single pass because vocabulary size is bounded
Stopword removal can be skipped because rare terms never appear in large corpora
Compression is unnecessary because sub-linear growth keeps the index small

questions.explanationMd: Heap's Law implies that new terms continue to appear as the corpus grows, even if the growth is sub-linear; indexing systems therefore need to handle vocabulary and index updates over time.

questions.questionMd: In OpenSearch terminology, which abstraction is most analogous to a schema definition in a relational database — specifying the field names, data types, and analyzers for stored documents?

options.text: A mapping.
A segment.
An index.
A setting.

questions.explanationMd: An OpenSearch mapping defines fields, data types, and analyzers, serving a role similar to a relational schema.

questions.questionMd: Crawling, text preprocessing, and index construction are all classified as offline pipeline stages. What is the primary architectural reason for this design choice?

options.text: Online stages require specialised hardware that cannot also execute indexing workloads
Offline stages consume too much RAM to run concurrently with live query traffic
Building the index in advance allows online query processing to complete within strict millisecond latency budgets
Preprocessing must be performed after each user query to reflect the most recent document versions

questions.explanationMd: Expensive crawling and indexing are performed before query time so that online retrieval can respond quickly using the prepared index.

questions.questionMd: In OpenSearch's text analysis pipeline, what is the correct order of processing stages?

options.text: Tokenizer → Character filters → Token filters
Character filters → Token filters → Tokenizer
Token filters → Tokenizer → Character filters
Character filters → Tokenizer → Token filters

questions.explanationMd: Character filters modify the raw text first, the tokenizer splits it into tokens, and token filters then transform those tokens.

questions.questionMd: In Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG), relevance scores are divided by the log base-2 of `(rank + 1)`. What user behavior does this logarithmic discount model?

options.text: Users prefer documents that are only marginally relevant at high ranks over highly relevant documents at low ranks
User attention diminishes at lower ranks, so a relevant document at rank 10 is worth less than one at rank 1
The discount penalizes systems that retrieve more than `k` documents, keeping result sets short
Users read results in random order, so position should have no effect on contribution

questions.explanationMd: The logarithmic discount models the fact that users pay more attention to higher-ranked results and less attention to lower-ranked ones.

questions.questionMd: A developer indexes a document in OpenSearch and immediately issues a search query but does not find the new document. Which concept best explains this behavior?

options.text: Near-real-time search requires a refresh before newly indexed documents become searchable.
Documents are only searchable after a full fsync commit, which occurs at most once per minute by default.
The document must be replicated to all replica shards before it can appear in search results.
Search queries skip the in-memory buffer by design; new documents are invisible until a segment merge completes.

questions.explanationMd: OpenSearch is near-real-time: newly indexed documents usually become searchable after a refresh creates a searchable segment.

questions.questionMd: What must a developer do in code when computing `NDCG@k` for a query that has no relevant documents in the collection?

options.text: Exclude that query from the evaluation and reduce `Q` by 1 in the MAP formula
Assign each retrieved document a relevance grade of 1 and recompute normally
Return `1.0`, because a system cannot be penalised for a query with no correct answers
Return `0.0` as a special-case guard, because `IDCG = 0` makes the formula undefined

questions.explanationMd: NDCG divides by ideal DCG. If no relevant documents exist, `IDCG` is zero, so implementations must handle this edge case explicitly.

questions.questionMd: A rare term appears in only one shard of a 5-shard OpenSearch index. Without any correction, how does this affect BM25 scoring for that term?

options.text: The term is assigned a zero IDF score because the coordinating node cannot find it on all shards simultaneously.
The term receives a lower-than-global IDF because each shard divides its local IDF by the total number of shards.
The shard containing that term computes an artificially high IDF because its local document count is much smaller than the global total.
The term is excluded from scoring because OpenSearch requires a term to appear on at least two shards to be indexed.

questions.explanationMd: If IDF is computed shard-locally, a rare term on one shard can look rarer than it is globally because the local shard has a smaller document population.

questions.questionMd: Which statement correctly describes a key theoretical difference between BM25 and TF-IDF with cosine similarity?

options.text: BM25 is a purely heuristic method, while TF-IDF has a formal probabilistic derivation from the Robertson-Sparck Jones weight
BM25 is derived from the Binary Independence Model and the Probability Ranking Principle, while TF-IDF is a heuristic weighting scheme
Both BM25 and TF-IDF are derived from the Binary Independence Model but differ only in their length normalization
TF-IDF is derived from the Probability Ranking Principle, while BM25 is an empirical approximation with no theoretical basis

questions.explanationMd: BM25 has a probabilistic motivation through BIM and the Probability Ranking Principle; TF-IDF cosine scoring is mainly a heuristic vector-space weighting scheme.

questions.questionMd: The k-gram index built over vocabulary terms serves two distinct retrieval functions in Week 3. Which pair correctly identifies both?

options.text: Phrase query position verification and proximity query distance checking
Wildcard query resolution and spelling correction candidate retrieval
Query optimization by document frequency and skip pointer construction
Biword index construction and permuterm rotation lookup

questions.explanationMd: K-gram indexes can retrieve vocabulary candidates matching wildcard patterns and can also generate candidates for spelling correction.

questions.questionMd: In the BSBI algorithm, after each RAM-sized block is processed and written to disk, what operation combines all on-disk blocks into the final inverted index?

options.text: A hash join that matches term_ids across blocks using an in-memory lookup table
A second full pass over the original corpus to resolve term_id collisions
A binary search tree insertion that merges block entries one term at a time
An external k-way merge sort over all sorted block files

questions.explanationMd: BSBI sorts each block and writes it to disk, then merges the sorted block files using an external k-way merge.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, which traversal strategy is the standard approach in modern IR systems for accumulating TF-IDF scores?

options.text: TAAT (Term At A Time), which processes one term across all matching documents before moving to the next
TAAT (Term At A Time), which is faster because it avoids the need for a score accumulator
DAAT (Document At A Time), which processes one document at a time and accumulates scores in a dictionary
DAAT (Document At A Time), which processes all terms in a document simultaneously before moving to the next document

questions.explanationMd: The lecture identifies DAAT as the standard traversal strategy, where scoring is organized around candidate documents and accumulated for ranking.

questions.questionMd: A proximity query is written as `term1 /k term2`. Which condition must hold in a candidate document for it to be included in the result?

options.text: `term1` must appear exactly `k` positions before `term2` in every occurrence
The terms must appear in the same sentence and within `k` paragraphs of each other
The positional difference between `term1` and `term2` must be at most `k`
The total count of `term1` and `term2` occurrences in the document must equal `k`

questions.explanationMd: A proximity query requires the two terms to occur within a specified positional distance, not exactly `k` positions apart.

questions.questionMd: Which statement correctly identifies a limitation of BSBI that SPIMI does not share?

options.text: BSBI requires a global term-to-integer dictionary to be maintained across all blocks
BSBI cannot handle corpora larger than available RAM because it performs no disk-based operations
BSBI sorts each block's postings list only once, making it slower than SPIMI's repeated sorting
BSBI appends doc_ids directly to hash-map postings lists, causing memory fragmentation

questions.explanationMd: BSBI depends on a global term-to-termID mapping, whereas SPIMI can build term dictionaries directly within blocks and avoid this global dictionary requirement.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following is a fundamental limitation of Boolean retrieval that motivates the move to ranked retrieval?

options.text: A document matching 3 out of 4 query terms is assumed as irrelevant as one matching 0 terms
Boolean retrieval is unable to handle OR operators between query terms
Boolean retrieval requires all query terms to be stemmed before matching
Boolean retrieval cannot use an inverted index to look up postings lists

questions.explanationMd: Boolean retrieval uses exact set membership rather than graded relevance, so partial matches can be treated the same as non-matches.

questions.questionMd: On a log-log plot of term rank vs. term frequency, what shape does Zipf's Law predict?

options.text: An S-shaped logistic curve
A straight line with a positive slope
A straight line with a slope of approximately -1
A concave curve that levels off as rank increases

questions.explanationMd: Zipf's Law predicts frequency is roughly inversely proportional to rank, which appears as a line with slope about -1 on a log-log plot.

questions.questionMd: Three terms are compared for VB compression efficiency: a high-frequency term appearing in 45 documents, a medium-frequency term in 15 documents, and a rare term in 3 documents. Which achieves the highest compression ratio and why?

options.text: The rare term, because fewer postings entries means less data to compress overall
The high-frequency term
All three achieve identical compression ratios because VB encoding is independent of term frequency
The medium-frequency term, because it balances gap size and postings list length optimally

questions.explanationMd: High-frequency terms often have denser postings lists with smaller gaps, which VB gap encoding can compress more effectively in ratio terms.

questions.questionMd: Using a permuterm index, how is the wildcard query `*tion` translated before performing a dictionary lookup?

options.text: It is decomposed into k-grams and an intersection query is run against the k-gram index
It is reversed to `noit*` and a suffix scan is performed on the dictionary
It is rotated to `tion$*` and then a prefix lookup is performed on `tion$`
It is padded to `$*tion$` and an exact match is performed in the permuterm dictionary

questions.explanationMd: In a permuterm index, the term is imagined with `$`; moving the wildcard to the end turns `*tion` into a prefix search for `tion$`.

questions.questionMd: A student runs a Porter stemmer and observes that both `"universe"` and `"university"` produce the stem `"univers"`. This is an example of which failure mode?

options.text: Under-stemming, which reduces retrieval recall
Accent folding, which merges morphologically unrelated forms
Incorrect case folding applied before stemming
Over-stemming, which reduces retrieval precision

questions.explanationMd: Over-stemming incorrectly merges distinct terms, which can retrieve irrelevant documents and reduce precision.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, the NLTK WordNetLemmatizer called on the word `"ran"` without providing a POS tag will produce which incorrect output?

options.text: `"go"`, because it links irregular verb forms through WordNet
`"runn"`, because it applies a heuristic suffix-stripping rule
`"run"`, because it correctly identifies the past tense
`"ran"` unchanged, because it defaults to treating the word as a noun

questions.explanationMd: Without a POS tag, WordNetLemmatizer defaults to noun behavior, so it does not convert the past-tense verb `ran` to `run`.

questions.questionMd: Document A has 1000 tokens and mentions `"space"` 10 times. Document B has 100 tokens and mentions `"space"` 5 times. Which claim about TF-IDF scoring is correct?

options.text: Both documents receive identical TF-IDF scores because IDF is the same for both
Document A scores higher because raw term count always dominates TF-IDF computation
Document B scores higher because its relative term frequency (5%) exceeds Document A's (1%)
Document A scores higher because a larger document contains more contextual evidence

questions.explanationMd: When term frequency is considered relative to document length or normalized, 5 occurrences in 100 tokens is stronger evidence than 10 occurrences in 1000 tokens.

questions.questionMd: After applying the full preprocessing pipeline (tokenize → lowercase → stopword removal → Porter stemming) to the input `"The astronauts ORBITING the International Space Station"`, which term in the output best illustrates a known over-stemming problem?

options.text: `"intern"` produced from `"International"`
`"astronaut"` produced from `"astronauts"`
`"space"` produced from `"Space"`
`"station"` produced from `"Station"`

questions.explanationMd: Porter stemming can reduce `international` to `intern`, which is a misleading merge with the word `intern` and is an over-stemming example.

questions.questionMd: Compared to the original forward dictionary, approximately how much larger does the permuterm index grow?

options.text: Roughly 4 to 5 times larger
The same size, since rotations are stored as pointers rather than full strings
Roughly 10 times larger
Roughly 2 times larger

questions.explanationMd: A permuterm index stores multiple rotations for each vocabulary term, so it is several times larger than the original dictionary.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture notes, where do the document frequency (`df`) values required for both TF-IDF and BM25 computation come from at retrieval time?

options.text: From the inverted index constructed during indexing, specifically from the length of each term's postings list
From a separate per-document frequency table computed fresh at query time by scanning the corpus
From the average document length statistic `avgdl` stored alongside the inverted index
From the query itself, by counting how many query terms appear in a predefined stopword list

questions.explanationMd: The inverted index stores a postings list for each term; the number of documents in that list gives the document frequency.

questions.questionMd: The NLTK English stopword list contains approximately how many words, and what is the approximate size of Lucene's default stopword list?

options.text: 500 words in NLTK and approximately 100 in Lucene
33 words in NLTK and approximately 179 in Lucene
179 words in NLTK and approximately 33 in Lucene
179 words in NLTK and approximately 179 in Lucene

questions.explanationMd: The lecture notes contrast the larger NLTK English stopword list, about 179 words, with Lucene's smaller default list, about 33 words.

questions.questionMd: A corpus has `N = 100,000` tokens. Using Heap's Law with `k = 44` and `β = 0.49`, what is the approximate predicted vocabulary size?

options.text: Approximately 4,400 unique terms
Approximately 44,000 unique terms
Approximately 13,600 unique terms
Approximately 100,000 unique terms

questions.explanationMd: Heap's Law estimates `V = kN^β`; substituting the given values gives a vocabulary size on the order of thirteen thousand unique terms.

questions.questionMd: In the Boolean retrieval model, what does a query return?

options.text: A probability distribution over matching documents
A set of document IDs with no ordering or relevance scores
A set of document IDs sorted by term frequency
A ranked list of documents sorted by relevance score

questions.explanationMd: Boolean retrieval returns an unordered set of documents that satisfy the Boolean expression, not a ranked list.

questions.questionMd: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between a token, a type, and a term?

options.text: A token is one occurrence in text; a type is a unique word form; a term is a normalized type entering the index
A token and a type are interchangeable; a term is produced only after stopword removal
A term is one occurrence in text; a token is a unique normalized form; a type is what enters the index
A type is one occurrence in text; a token is a unique word form; a term is produced by tokenization

questions.explanationMd: Tokens are individual occurrences, types are distinct surface forms, and terms are normalized forms used in the index.

questions.questionMd: In SMART notation, the scheme `lnc.ltc` specifies which combination of weighting choices for documents and queries respectively?

options.text: Documents use natural TF, cosine normalization, no IDF; queries use log-TF, IDF, cosine normalization
Documents use log-TF, natural IDF, cosine normalization; queries use log-TF, no IDF, cosine normalization
Documents use log-TF, no IDF, no normalization; queries use log-TF, standard IDF, cosine normalization
Documents use log-TF, no IDF, cosine normalization; queries use log-TF, standard IDF, cosine normalization

questions.explanationMd: In `lnc.ltc`, documents use logarithmic TF, no IDF, and cosine normalization; queries use logarithmic TF, IDF, and cosine normalization.

questions.questionMd: Why is Normalized DCG (NDCG) preferred over raw DCG when comparing results across multiple queries?

options.text: NDCG normalizes by the ideal DCG so all queries map to `[0,1]`
NDCG uses binary relevance labels, which are easier to collect than the graded labels required by raw DCG
Raw DCG rewards retrieving more documents, while NDCG penalizes systems that return more than `k` results
NDCG applies a stricter position discount than DCG, making it more sensitive to early retrieval errors

questions.explanationMd: NDCG divides DCG by the ideal DCG for that query, making scores comparable across queries with different relevance distributions.

questions.questionMd: As the raw term frequency `tf` in a document increases toward infinity, what value does the BM25 TF saturation function `tf * (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1)` approach?

options.text: The value `k1 + 1`, which is the asymptotic maximum that the saturation function never exceeds
The value `k1`, which acts as a hard ceiling on TF contributions
The value `tf`, meaning the saturation function converges back to raw TF at very high counts
The value `1`, because the saturation function is normalized to the range `[0, 1]`

questions.explanationMd: As `tf` becomes very large, the leading `tf` terms dominate the numerator and denominator, so the expression approaches `k1 + 1`.

questions.questionMd: According to the lecture, in which of the following situations does the Bag-of-Words assumption most clearly lead to incorrect retrieval behavior?

options.text: When two documents have the same vocabulary size, because BoW cannot differentiate their vectors
When query terms appear frequently in the same document, because BoW over-weights high-frequency terms
When a query contains negation such as `"not relevant"`
When query terms are stopwords, because BoW assigns them the same weight as content terms

questions.explanationMd: Bag-of-Words ignores word order and syntax, so it can mishandle negation; `not relevant` may be treated similarly to `relevant`.

questions.questionMd: Which sequence correctly describes the three-stage spelling correction pipeline?

options.text: K-gram candidate retrieval → edit distance ranking → Jaccard similarity filtering
Edit distance ranking → Jaccard similarity filtering → k-gram candidate retrieval
Jaccard similarity filtering → k-gram candidate retrieval → edit distance ranking
K-gram candidate retrieval → Jaccard similarity filtering → edit distance ranking

questions.explanationMd: The pipeline first uses k-grams to retrieve candidates, filters them by Jaccard similarity, and then ranks remaining candidates using edit distance.

questions.questionMd: Heap's Law describes how vocabulary size `V` grows with the total number of tokens `N` in a corpus. Which statement correctly characterizes this growth?

options.text: Vocabulary grows sub-linearly and never fully stops growing
Vocabulary grows linearly, adding a fixed number of new terms per document
Vocabulary grows exponentially in proportion to the square of `N`
Vocabulary growth stops once the corpus exceeds a threshold size

questions.explanationMd: Heap's Law states `V = kN^β` with `0 < β < 1`, so vocabulary growth is sub-linear but continues as the corpus grows.
